title: Note on the Reformulation for Static Robust Problems for Convex Uncertainty Sets
contribution: A five-page note (May 17, 2015) with revised proofs of three reformulation lemmas of a published adaptive-RO paper (S176 by page range and notation, my inference): the static robust value min{λ : λb ≥ d, b ∈ conv T(U, h)} and its extensions now hold for general convex, compact, down-monotone uncertainty sets, not only polytopes.
problem_entry: {RO+LO} The original proofs assume a polytope while the results are stated for convex, compact, down-monotone sets; the note supplies proofs for the general case (p. 1).
key_idea: Replace the extreme-point argument by support-function/gauge duality: robust rows over U_j ⇔ one constraint over conv(∪U_j) = conv T(U, h); the static value is the support function of (conv T)° ∩ Rⁿ₊, rewritten as a gauge (pp. 1–2); Lemmas 6 and 8 reduce to Lemma 4 by lifting v = (y, µ + 1) (pp. 2–4).
assumptions: Static robust packing LP max{dᵀy : By ≤ h ∀B ∈ U, y ≥ 0}, h > 0 (p. 1); objective uncertainty through a product set U^B × U^d (p. 2); joint (B, h) uncertainty with the h_j = 0 case trivial (pp. 3–4). No data.
proof_devices: robust row constraints over all U_j equal one constraint over conv(∪U_j) = conv T(U, h), by Theorem 3 of the parent paper (p. 1)
support function of C = (conv T)° ∩ Rⁿ₊ rewritten as the Minkowski functional of C°, via Hiriart-Urruty–Lemaréchal Prop. 3.2.5 and polar identities (pp. 1–2)
lifting v = (y, µ + 1) reduces objective uncertainty (Lemma 6) and joint (B, h) uncertainty (Lemma 8) to Lemma 4 (pp. 2–4)
row normalization by h_j likened to the perspective function to keep convexity (p. 4); substitution θ_j = (µ_j/h_j)/Σ µ_i/h_i (p. 5)
[my reading] the identity printed as (S1 ∩ S2)° = S1° ∪ S2° needs the closed convex hull of the union; the final form λb ≥ d is what that hull gives (p. 2)
positioning: Corrects the authors' own published lemmas (cited only by page numbers 291, 298, 304, 318, which fall in S176's print range, my inference); cites only Hiriart-Urruty–Lemaréchal and Boyd–Vandenberghe for the convex-analysis facts (pp. 1–2, 4–5).
writing: One opening sentence says what is revised and why (the polytope assumption); the rest is three proofs in sequence, each closed by 'which completes the proof' (pp. 1–5).
limits_future: Repairs proofs only; does not say whether any published statement changes. Whether it was issued as a formal erratum cannot be told from the file (not checked).

method_links.note: The static robust value is read off a dual object (a gauge over conv T), and the reformulation is extended from polytopes to the convex sets the theorems claim.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: proof-repair note keeping the published statements
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: revised proofs of Lemmas 4, 6 and 8 circulated as a dated note because the originals assumed a polytope; the statements are kept, unlike the claim-narrowing correction of Workflow E

transferable: To robustify a packing LP over a convex, non-polyhedral uncertainty set, write the robust feasible set as the polar of conv(∪ row sets) intersected with the orthant; its support function is the gauge min{λ : λb ≥ d, b ∈ conv T} (pp. 1–2).
To add objective or right-hand-side uncertainty to such a result, lift the variables (v = (y, µ + 1)) so the new case is the old lemma in one more dimension (pp. 2–4).

quotes.text: The original proof in the paper assume that the uncertainty is a polytope.
Note that the last maximization problem can be viewed as the support function of the set

title: Reformulation versus cutting-planes for robust optimization: A computational study
contribution: A statistical benchmark of duality-based reformulation against cutting planes for robust LO and MIO with budget and ellipsoidal sets (183 LO and 40 MIO instances): neither dominates, contradicting Fischetti–Monaci for robust MIO, and a hybrid that runs both in parallel cuts run times to 50–75% of any single method.
problem_entry: {RO+IO+LO} Two standard solution routes for RO and 'little guidance' on which to use; the one prior study (Fischetti–Monaci 2012) covered only polyhedral sets, without significance tests or cutting-plane variants; the question is reframed for parallel computing (p. 2).
key_idea: Specify the RMIO cutting-plane method (root cuts, lazy constraints at integer solutions, a repair heuristic that fixes integers and solves an RLO by cuts) (pp. 5–7), benchmark all variants with robust statistics (pp. 10–11), then evaluate a hybrid that takes the first method to finish (pp. 16–20).
assumptions: Constraint-wise budget sets (at most Γ deviations; Γ glyph dropped in the file, my reading) and ellipsoids (pp. 3, 8–9); NETLIB, Mittelmann, MIPLIB3 and MIPLIB 2010 'easy' instances; coefficients uncertain unless simple rationals, 2% deviations, equality rows certain; 183 LO and 40 MIO instances; results reported for Γ = 5 (pp. 9–11).
proof_devices: class map: reformulation LO/MIO for budget sets and SOCP/MISOCP for ellipsoids; cutting-plane master LO/MIO for both (Table 1, p. 8)
budget-set separation by partial sorting in O(n + Γ log Γ) (p. 8); ellipsoid separation in closed form from KKT in O(n) (p. 9)
finite termination via finitely many extreme points for polyhedral sets; none guaranteed for ellipsoids (p. 9)
one-variable counterexample: a robust-feasible root relaxation with no robust integer solution (p. 5)
lazy constraints at integer candidates plus a repair heuristic that fixes the integers and solves the remaining RLO by cuts (pp. 6–7)
experiments: Gurobi 5.6, C++, one thread, 1,000 s (pp. 4, 10); % fastest, median and geometric mean of run time over per-instance best, bootstrap CIs, performance profiles (pp. 10–11). RLO-budget: cuts fastest on 75.5% but best-of-both reformulation geo-mean 1.39 vs 1.52 (p. 12); RLO-ellipsoid: reformulation 1.38 vs 1.76 (p. 13); RMIO: no significant winner (p. 14); root cuts essential on infeasible instances (p. 16); repair heuristic no average gain (pp. 16, 18); hybrid 50–75% of single-method time (pp. 18, 22). Not stated: treatment of time-outs, code release (my reading).
positioning: Replicates and extends Fischetti–Monaci (2012): agrees for RLO with budget sets, contradicts their 'significantly worse' verdict on cutting planes for RMIO, and attributes the difference to the test set, root cuts or metrics (pp. 2, 11, 14); borrows the racing idea from Gurobi's concurrent LP and suggests ROME as a home for it (pp. 2–3).
writing: Numbered contribution list (p. 3); every comparison stated with its confidence interval and hedged ('too small to confidently declare as significant', p. 14); one summary bullet per problem class in the discussion (p. 22).
limits_future: Hybrid not implemented as a tool (p. 2) and evaluated assuming no interference between simultaneous single-thread runs (p. 20); thread allocation instance-specific (p. 21); MISOCP solvers young (p. 16). Future: tougher MIO instances, stabilization, warm starts, presolve, block structure (p. 23).

method_links.note: The class-keeping device is the cutting-plane master (LO/MIO even for ellipsoids), and the route is chosen by measured run times rather than by problem class.

A duel between two exact methods on public libraries with solver version, threads, limit and CIs stated; no heuristic incumbent, and the hybrid is a computed minimum of separate runs, not run as one solver.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: race the rival methods instead of ranking them
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the which-is-better question is replaced by a parallel portfolio that stops at the first finisher, modelled on concurrent LP; its time is reported as a ratio to each single method

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: head-to-head study of rival solution paradigms with statistical testing
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: medians and geometric means of normalized run times with bootstrap CIs and performance profiles; a second case in this batch is S197

transferable: Report benchmark run times as ratios to the per-instance best, summarized by median and geometric mean with bootstrap CIs, beside performance profiles; do not average ratios arithmetically (pp. 10–11).
When no method dominates, evaluate the portfolio that runs them in parallel and stops at the first finisher, and report its time as a ratio to each single method (pp. 16–19).

In a cutting-plane MIO with semi-infinite constraints, separate at the root until the relaxation is feasible, then only at integer candidates (lazy constraints); analyze infeasible instances separately (pp. 6, 15–16).

quotes.text: There is little guidance in the literature about which method should be used for any given RO problem instance.
This is a clear win, and suggests that a hypothetical robust optimization solver should follow this hybrid strategy.

title: Unified optimization of traffic flows through airports
contribution: A two-phase binary IP that jointly chooses runway configurations, runway assignments and sequences, gate holding and taxi and terminal-airspace routes; flight-type-indexed variables keep it solvable, real DFW and BOS days solve in typically five to 10 minutes with phase differences of at most 2.1%, and surface times fall 5–14% (DFW) and 7–25% (BOS) against history.
problem_entry: {IO+AP} Airport decisions are optimized one subproblem at a time, which 'may lead to overall solutions which are grossly suboptimal, or indeed infeasible'; ATFM work focuses on network flows; delays cost US airlines $8.3 billion in 2007 (pp. 2–4).
key_idea: P1 (runways as the bottleneck, other capacities relaxed) indexes sequencing variables by flight type because separation depends only on type: O(CRT + FR) variables and O(C²RT) constraints instead of O(FRT) and O(F²RT) (p. 6); P2 fixes P1's assignments and orders and routes flights with 'by' variables (pp. 9–11).
assumptions: Deterministic inputs, one-hour horizon in 20 s periods (pp. 4–5, 12); close parallel runways as one runway, '(only slightly) conservative' (p. 7); P2 feasible without strict deadlines (pp. 5, 9). Data: one day each at DFW (Nov 2, 2009) and BOS (Sept 28, 2010) from METAR, ASDE-X and ASPM; releases at actual pushback and touchdown times (pp. 12, 14).
proof_devices: flight-type-indexed sequencing variables: O(CRT + FR) variables and O(C²RT) constraints instead of O(FRT) and O(F²RT) (p. 6)
cumulative counting constraints (2i) link type slots to individual flights; a flight sequence always exists when deadlines are not strict (pp. 7–8)
Proposition 1: valid inequalities (3)–(5) for conv(X), not valid for the LP relaxation; proof in the online appendix (p. 9)
'by' variables with separation as dominance constraints only for pairs adjacent in P1, facet-defining for a similar problem (Bertsimas–Stock-Patterson) (pp. 10–11)
fork, joint and antichain inequalities from Bertsimas–Lulli–Odoni (p. 12)
P1–P2 objective difference reported as a bound on the optimality gap (Tables 1–2, p. 13)
experiments: Gurobi 5.0, i7-860, 16 GB, 1,200 s per phase; eight one-hour instances per airport (153–175 flights at DFW, 59–91 at BOS); P1–P2 differences ≤ 2.1%, P1 gaps 0.0, totals 161–1,465 s (my decoding, p. 13); surface times −5–14% (DFW) and −7–25% (BOS) against the historical days, arrival taxi times up (p. 13); gate holding 10.1 vs 10.5 vs 11.3 min historical (p. 17). Text says other differences ≤ 1.1% but BOS row 6 decodes to 1.3% (pp. 12–13).
positioning: Extends Bertsimas–Frankovich–Odoni (2011, S120), criticizing its reliance on runway capacity envelopes (p. 3); positions against single-subproblem work (Gilbo; runway sequencing as a bounded traveling repairman problem after Tsitsiklis 1992; gate holding; taxi routing) (pp. 3–4); builds P2 on Bertsimas–Stock-Patterson 1998 and Bertsimas–Lulli–Odoni 2008 (pp. 10–12).
writing: Contribution stated as 'the first truly unified and tractable' approach (p. 4); barriers to implementation get a full paragraph in the introduction (p. 4); experiments are organized around three questions answered in a closing summary (pp. 12, 17).
limits_future: Deterministic data, no airline fairness, a central decision-maker against collaborative ATM, mixed time scales; only configuration-type decisions implementable today (pp. 4, 15, 17); surface times only, fix times unavailable (p. 13). Future: uncertainty and fairness (p. 17).

method_links.note: A problem practice splits into pieces is written as binary IPs with a device (type-indexed variables) that keeps them solvable at real scale; tractability shown as solve time on historical days; what is not modelled is named.
Solver gaps and run times per phase, and the phase difference as a gap for the decomposition; no heuristic incumbent is dueled.
Judged against the historical days, but with perfect knowledge of pushback and touchdown times, surface times only and no field test.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: type-indexed variables when the coupling depends only on type
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: separation depends only on weight class and orientation, so slot variables are indexed by type and linked to flights by counting constraints; claimed applicable to general bounded-TSP problems

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: relax-then-restrict decomposition with the phase difference as an optimality bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: P1 relaxes non-runway capacities, P2 restores them with P1's sequence fixed; the difference of the two optima is tabulated as a bound on the gap

transferable: When pairwise constraints (separation, setups) depend only on a few types, index time-slot variables by type and link them to individual jobs with cumulative counting constraints; constraints fall from O(F²RT) to O(C²RT) (pp. 6–8).

Decompose by the bottleneck: solve it with other capacities relaxed, fix its sequence, solve the full routing, and print the difference of the two optimal values as a bound on the loss (pp. 5, 9, 13).
In time-indexed routing, use cumulative variables equal to 1 once a flight has reached node j by time t, so that precedence and separation become dominance constraints between them (pp. 10–11).

quotes.text: a naïve attempt to solve this overall problem would be far from computationally tractable
Indeed, this modeling technique may be applied for general bounded-TSP type problems.

title: Decomposable Markov decision processes: A fluid optimization approach
contribution: A fluid LP over per-component state–action frequencies, linear in the number of components, whose re-solved policy is optimal under achievability; its bound is proved tighter than ALO, an alternate Lagrangian relaxation (shown equal to ALO) and the classical Lagrangian relaxation, and on bandits the policy beats greedy, ALR and the Bertsimas–Niño-Mora primal-dual heuristic.
problem_entry: {SD+LO} Product-form MDPs have exponential state spaces while data come per component; ALO keeps one constraint per state, Lagrangian relaxation needs a decomposable action space, and performance-region models are 'fragile' outside conservation laws (pp. 2–5).
key_idea: Variables x^m_ka(t) are marginal frequencies of component m in state k under system action a; per-component conservation plus action-consistency constraints; T periods exact and a discounted tail; re-solve and take arg max_a A_a(1) (pp. 6–8).
assumptions: Independent components, additive rewards, any action allowed in any state (p. 6). Bandits with identical rewards, M = 5, n = 4 (1,024 states) for exact bounds and M, n up to 20 for simulation; one deterministic-transition family called 'potentially pathological' (pp. 15–17).
proof_devices: a feasible fluid solution built from the optimal policy gives J* ≤ Z*_T; Z*_T non-increasing in T (Propositions 2 and 4, pp. 7–8)
Theorem 1: under achievability the policy greedy in A(1) is optimal (p. 7)
Theorem 2: alternate Lagrangian relaxation equals ALO in bound and value function, by mapping optimal solutions to feasible ones (p. 11)
Theorem 3 / Corollary 2: J* ≤ Z*_T ≤ … ≤ Z*_1 ≤ Z*_ALO = Z*_ALR ≤ Z*_CLR (p. 12)
Propositions 8–9: the Bertsimas–Niño-Mora performance-region bound equals CLR and ALR for bandits (p. 14)
experiments: Exact J* by value iteration: fluid bound closer than ALR on every instance and discount, little change beyond T = 5–10 (Tables 2–3, pp. 15–17). Simulation (500 steps, 100 initial states, β = 0.99): fluid policy beats greedy, ALR and the primal-dual heuristic; at M = n = 20 mean gap to the best bound about 1.2% vs 11.2%, 12.0% and 36.2% (my decoding, Table 5, p. 18), about 2.6 s per action (p. 19). Solver and hardware not named (my reading).
positioning: Tightens ALO (de Farias–Van Roy) and Lagrangian relaxation (Hawkins; Adelman–Mersereau), proving ALR = ALO; places the authors' own performance-region model (Bertsimas–Niño-Mora 1996, 2000) as equal to CLR and ALR and weaker than the fluid bound (pp. 4–5, 11–14).
writing: The main result is announced in the introduction as one displayed chain of inequalities (p. 3) and restated as Corollaries 2 and 4 (pp. 12, 14); each result is followed by a short proof idea, with proofs in the e-companion (pp. 7–8, 11–12).
limits_future: Exponential system action spaces not considered (p. 9); LP solution may not be achievable (p. 7); not the smallest formulation (p. 12). Future: robust or adaptive fluid models for uncertain data, and posterior sampling for learning (p. 19).

method_links.note: A dynamic-programming problem written as an LP linear in the number of components; equivalence theorems place the rival relaxations; the boundary (action spaces, achievability, size) is printed.
Simulated policies scored by their gap to the best upper bound and dueled against greedy, ALR and his own 2000 primal-dual heuristic; no warm start, no solver or machine named.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one chain of bounds for all rival relaxations
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: J* ≤ Z*_T ≤ … ≤ Z*_ALO = Z*_ALR ≤ Z*_CLR (= Z*_BNM for bandits) organizes the competing approaches in a single ordering

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: place your own earlier method in the new hierarchy and beat it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the Bertsimas–Niño-Mora (2000) performance-region bound is shown equal to CLR and ALR, and its primal-dual heuristic has the largest gaps in simulation

transferable: For a product-form MDP, write an LP over per-component state–action frequencies with an action-consistency constraint; take the action with the largest first-period frequency and re-solve every period (pp. 6–8).
Keep T periods disaggregated and aggregate the tail by a discounted conservation constraint; the bound improves monotonically in T, a dial between size and quality (pp. 7–8).
Score heuristic policies by the gap between simulated reward and the tightest available upper bound, so every policy gets a certificate-like number (p. 18).

quotes.text: This alternate Lagrangian relaxation is significant because it extends the scope of the Lagrangian relaxation approach to problems that do not have a decomposable system action space.
For such problems, the fluid formulation (3) will be harder to solve; we do not consider this regime in the present paper.

title: Scalable robust and adaptive inventory routing
contribution: Robust and affinely adaptive MIO for finite-horizon inventory routing with temperature-driven, non-convex demand uncertainty, made exact by a worst-case algorithm (Opt-Temp) and scaled to about 6,000 customers over 151 days by neighborhood routes, warm starts and constraint generation; stockouts fall by over 94% against the nominal model and the fleet can shrink from 11 to 8 vehicles.
problem_entry: {RO+IO+AP} Exact approaches solve only up to around a hundred customers and heuristics shorten the horizon (p. 3); the cited robust inventory-routing papers report 30 and 50 customers (p. 7), while a typical heating-oil company serves about 10,000; the company's main objective was a smaller fleet with schedules robust to demand (pp. 2–3).
key_idea: Routes as neighborhoods with a fixed visiting cost (pp. 8, 18); CLT-style sets on temperature and customer noise give a non-convex demand set (pp. 10–11); Opt-Temp computes the worst case exactly, so the robust model is a deterministic MIO with 2NT extra constraints (pp. 12–16); affine adaptive quantities solved by cutting planes with Opt-Temp as oracle (pp. 16–18).
assumptions: Demand convex piecewise-linear in temperature; Γ set for 99% temperature coverage for large T (pp. 10–11); projection onto the first t periods weakens the guarantees (p. 16). TSPLIB locations (51–5,915 customers), single depot, generated demand and initial levels, Boston temperatures Nov 2013–Mar 2014, 50 training and 50 test scenarios, T = 151 (pp. 20–22, 28–29).
proof_devices: Theorem 1 (Opt-Temp): exact maximization of an affine combination of convex non-increasing functions over a CLT budget set; an exchange argument leaves at most one interior temperature, then a sorted greedy (pp. 13–15)
robust constraints replaced by 2NT deterministic constraints built from worst-case demand sums (p. 16)
adaptive model solved by cutting planes with Opt-Temp as the separation oracle (pp. 17–18)
set-cover route improvement by column generation on its LP relaxation with reduced costs from the duals (pp. 19–20)
experiments: Gurobi 6.0.0 via JuMP, 16-core Xeon, 128 GB, two hours per model, warm-started nominal → robust → adaptive (pp. 21–22); stockouts from 160–225% of customers to under 9%, at least 94% per scenario and over 96% on average (p. 22); cost ratios robust/nominal 0.425–0.860 with Gurobi gaps 16–77% for robust and adaptive models (Table 1, p. 25); 24 h runs settle only the two smallest nominal models (pp. 24–25); fleet 11 → 8 at N = 575 without more stockouts (pp. 26–27). Savings above 100 customers given as 44% (p. 24) and 56% (p. 27); Table 1 supports 44% (my reading).
positioning: Against exact robust IRP methods (Solyali et al.: 30 customers; Aghezzaf: 50) claims two orders of magnitude more customers (p. 7); against stochastic and MDP approaches argues tractability and insensitivity to distributional assumptions (pp. 3, 6); chooses affine over finite adaptability for scalability (p. 7).
writing: Four labelled contributions (Robustness, Adaptability, Scalability, Quality of solutions) (pp. 3–4); headline percentages in the abstract (p. 1); the solver-gap caveat and the 24-hour check sit in the body (pp. 24–25).
limits_future: Neighborhood costs unsuited to link-dominated routing (p. 8); heuristic route generation, 'not the main focus' (p. 18); weakened probabilistic guarantees (p. 16); weak lower bounds (pp. 25, 28). Future: provable lower bounds (Bertsimas–de Ruiter), emergency-refuelling routing, dynamic quantities (p. 28).

method_links.note: A non-convex uncertainty set handled by an exact worst-case oracle, so the robust model stays a deterministic MIO and the adaptive model a cutting-plane MIO; scale stated in customers, days and hours.

Warm starts chained nominal → robust → adaptive; solver, limit and gaps printed even when large, with a 24-hour check whose failure on larger cases is reported; but the cost claims rest on solutions with 16–77% gaps.
Γ set by a coverage target and tuned on training scenarios, not published as a curve; the owner's knob, fleet size, gets a price table with its bad case (five vehicles or fewer).
The owner (a heating-oil company) set the objective, but the baseline is the nominal model on synthetic data, not the company's current schedules.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: coarsen the decision until the uncertainty layer scales
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: routes are neighborhoods with fixed visiting costs, which shrinks the route space, warm-starts from the company's routes and lets the robust and adaptive MIOs reach about 6,000 customers

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact worst case over a non-convex set by an exchange argument
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Opt-Temp: some optimum has at most one temperature strictly inside its bounds, so enumeration of that coordinate plus a sorted greedy is exact

transferable: To robustify against a common driver (temperature) plus individual noise, put CLT-style budget sets on both and compute each constraint's worst case by a sorted greedy with one interior coordinate (pp. 10–15).
Warm-start each richer model with the previous one's solution so it is feasible from the start: robust quantities become the adaptive base amounts with zero affine terms (p. 22).
When gaps stay large, rerun the smallest instances for 24 hours and report whether the solutions changed (pp. 24–25).

quotes.text: Our robust and adaptive formulations are tractable for ∼6000 customers.
This weakens the theoretical probabilistic guarantees that we can make, because the Central Limit Theorem might not apply in small cases.

title: Moneyball for professors: models for predicting research impact
contribution: A four-page MIT IDE research brief of the Tenure Analytics paper (S206): network-centrality models built on a scholar's first five years predict later research impact better than citation counts, and at equal capacity their tenure picks differ from committees' in 16 of 54 cases with better later research records.
problem_entry: {DA+ML+AP} Tenure and funding decisions rest on subjective assessments, and the h-index family remains the quantitative standard; the authors call for a 'Moneyball moment' in academia (p. 1).
key_idea: Centrality in citation, coauthorship and combined networks from the first five years feeds predictions; ranking scholars and labelling the top 35 the models' tenure selections (as many as the committees tenured, 35 of 54) turns predictions into decisions comparable with the committees' (pp. 2–3).
assumptions: 198,310 OR papers 1975–2012 (p. 1); hand-built funnel 685 → 203 → 75 → 61 scholars (35 tenured), 54 in the comparison; outcomes at 9 and 16 years (pp. 2–3). The brief names no model class and does not explain 61 → 54 (my reading); S206's card records random forests.
experiments: Agreement with committees on 38 of 54 (70%), eight swapped each way; the model's picks have better A-journal counts, citations and h-indexes and do not differ significantly in awards, editorships, subfield, gender or coauthor counts (pp. 2–4); gain sizes only in Figure 2, which has no text layer (my reading).
positioning: Positions against the h-index and its variants (Hirsch 2005; Podsakoff et al.) and against subjective committee practice (p. 1); defers all detail to the OR Forum paper (S206) (p. 1).
writing: Research-brief format: four bullet takeaways and pull quotes in capitals (pp. 1–2, 4); 'Moneyball' framing (p. 1); the limitations take as much space as the findings (p. 4).
limits_future: Small n; the tenure decision may change later outcomes; fixed tenure slots as a simplification; OR and top programmes only; gaming of centrality would force recalibration (p. 4). Future: other fields, hiring, grants and awards; a service on Google Scholar or Web of Science (p. 4).

method_links.note: Decisions, not predictions, are scored against the owner's current rule (committee decisions) at equal capacity; the model is offered as a decision aid, with what the backtest cannot show printed.

transferable: To compare a predictor with human decisions, fix the number of positive decisions at the humans' number (35 of 54), rank by prediction, and compare the outcomes of the two selections and of the disagreements (p. 3).
Before claiming the model's picks are better, check that they do not differ on the criteria the model ignores (awards, gender, subfield) (p. 4).
coauthors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Shachar Reichman, John Silberholz

quotes.text: It remains to be seen whether these models can be useful to tenure committees

If models relying on network centrality gain widespread use in the tenure decision-making process, we expect that candidates might change their publication behavior to boost their centrality in citation and co-authorship networks, prompting further recalibration of the proposed model.

title: Robust product line design
contribution: Robust product line design that maximizes worst-case expected revenue over an uncertainty set of choice models, covering parameter uncertainty (bootstrap, posterior or polyhedral sets) and structural uncertainty (several fitted model structures); on a real conjoint data set nominal lines lose up to 23% (parameter) and 37% (structure) in the worst case, and robust lines improve worst-case revenue by up to 14% and 55%.
problem_entry: {RO+IO+AP; ML for estimation, HS as solver} PLD assumes a known choice model, but it is estimated from small conjoint samples; parameter and structural uncertainty; product lines are hard to reverse (pp. 2–3). Prior work: a post hoc robustness test (Belloni et al., 2–5% loss) and MNL-specific robust assortment (pp. 4–6).
key_idea: Plug the worst-case revenue over a set of choice models into the standard divide-and-conquer heuristic (pp. 8–9); build the set from bootstraps, posterior draws, EM local optima, polyhedral segment weights (worst case an LP for first-choice models) or structurally distinct models (pp. 9–11); trace a frontier with α·worst case + (1 − α)·nominal (p. 11).
assumptions: First-choice, latent-class MNL and hierarchical-Bayes mixture MNL models (pp. 6–7); Toubia et al. (2003) Timbuk2 conjoint data: 330 respondents, 10 attributes, 3,584 products, lines of 5, three competitor bags as no-purchase, Belloni et al.'s revenues (p. 12); B = 100 bootstraps, MCMC with 100,000 iterations (pp. 13, 15).
proof_devices: worst-case objective as a minimum over a finite set of models, or an LP for first-choice models with polyhedral segment weights (pp. 8–10)
ordering of nominal and robust solutions in the nominal and worst cases derived from optimality; the experiments use heuristic solutions, so it is not guaranteed there (my reading) (pp. 9, 12)
constraint form (21) and weighted form (22) of the nominal–robust trade-off; the weighted form keeps existing heuristics usable (p. 11)
experiments: Julia, custom EM, R bayesm; divide-and-conquer from 10 random starts, no gaps or run times (p. 12); metrics WCL and RI (p. 12). Parameter: WCL up to 23.02%, RI 0.36–13.82% across K (Table 2, pp. 13–14); box sets WCL 2.38% at ε = 0.2 and 10.11% at ε = 2 (p. 13). Structural: WCL 23–37%, RI 13.7–54.6%, robust revenue $63.38–$63.69 under all three models (Table 5, p. 18); Pareto frontier for K = 8 (p. 15).
positioning: Contrasts with nominal PLD (Zufryden; Green–Krieger; Kohli–Sukumar; Belloni et al.), with Sawtooth's randomized first-choice model, which 'does not address uncertainty in a worst-case way', and with Rusmevichientong–Topaloglu's MNL-specific robust assortment (pp. 4–6); structural uncertainty credited to his own prostate-screening paper (pp. 3, 6).
writing: Two numbered contributions with headline numbers (p. 3); a hypothetical illustration (Figure 1) motivates the worst case over the average (p. 9); each experiment section ends by interpreting why RI behaves as it does (pp. 14, 18–19).
limits_future: One data set, heuristic solutions only, continuous MNL sets left out as hard (p. 11; my reading for the first two). Future: cost uncertainty and competitive responses in the no-purchase option (p. 19).

method_links.note: Robustness priced by WCL and RI, a set-size knob ε and an α-weighted frontier, with the weak case printed (RI 0.36% at K = 4); no solution-independent bound, and the curve is computed heuristically.
An IO problem solved only heuristically (divide-and-conquer from 10 random starts) with no gap or certificate; the exact MIO came later for the nominal first-choice case (S093, card in c2-04).
The robust version keeps the nominal problem's heuristic, and the worst case is an LP for first-choice models with polyhedral weights; the class kept is a heuristic's, not a solver's.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: structural uncertainty: robustness over a set of fitted model structures
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the uncertainty set contains a first-choice and two LCMNL models of similar fit; the idea is imported from a prostate-screening paper and gives a line that performs evenly under all three

transferable: Build the uncertainty set from the estimation itself (bootstrap re-fits, posterior draws, EM local optima); the worst case over a finite set is the minimum of B evaluations (pp. 9–10).
When model-selection criteria disagree (AIC against CAIC), optimize against the worst of the 'good enough' models instead of picking one (pp. 16–18).
Report the worst-case loss of the nominal solution and the relative improvement of the robust one, and trace the nominal-against-worst-case frontier with a weighted objective (pp. 11–12, 15).

quotes.text: Almost all approaches to PLD tacitly assume that this choice model is known precisely and is beyond suspicion.
In summary: the robust solution will perform better than the nominal solution in the worst case, while the nominal solution will perform better than the robust solution in the nominal case.

title: A comparison of Monte Carlo tree search and rolling horizon optimization for large-scale dynamic resource allocation problems
contribution: A matched-budget comparison of Monte Carlo tree search and rolling-horizon (fluid) optimization on tactical wildfire management and queueing network control: both beat simple baselines and are comparable on small instances, while RHO gains the edge as instances grow, especially in action space; journal version of S340 with queueing and inexact-calibration experiments added.
problem_entry: {SD+HS+IO; AP as testbed} AI's MCTS and OR's RHO each succeed on dynamic stochastic problems, but 'the relative merits of these two approaches are not well understood'; MCTS's successes are in games with small branching, while a wildfire instance branches about 230 million ways (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: MCTS with double progressive widening, a GA-style action generator and strong rollouts (FW heuristic; cμ) (pp. 6–7) against a deterministic smoothed MIO (fire) or the Avram–Bertsimas–Ricard fluid policy (queues), re-solved each period (pp. 4–5); compared at matched budgets with significance tests (pp. 8–11).
assumptions: Wildfire MDP on a k × k grid, p = 0.06, suppression success 0.8, identical teams, no travel time (pp. 3, 8); queueing networks with Poisson arrivals and exponential services (criss-cross, six-class, extended six-class and reentrant with 2–7 servers), parameters from S244 (pp. 3, 12–14); synthetic instances only.
proof_devices: smoothed deterministic intensity dynamics written as an MIO with binary team assignments and fuel-exhaustion flags, re-solved each period; stated not to be the original problem (pp. 4–5)
action branching factor counted with Stirling's approximation (p. 11)
additive-effects regressions with p-values for hyperparameters and method comparisons (Tables 2–4, pp. 8–11)
experiments: C++ MCTS, Gurobi 5.0, 2.2 GHz single-thread cores, 256 simulations per setting (pp. 7–8); MCTS given 60/90/120 s against RHO's ≤ 120 s (pp. 9, 11); RHO's fitted gain over FW exceeds every MCTS budget's (Table 3, p. 10); at k = 20 MCTS falls below FW with 16 or 32 teams while RHO beats FW throughout (Table 4, p. 11); sampled-transition RHO matches exact RHO (p. 12); queues: fluid best on the reentrant network (54.711 vs 63.696 at m = 7), MCTS ahead of fluid for m = 3–6 on the extended six-class network where cμ is usually best (pp. 13–14); fluid queue results reused from the 2015 paper's C code (p. 12).
positioning: Frames itself between AI (Coulom; Kocsis–Szepesvári; Browne et al.; progressive widening of Couëtoux et al.) and OR fluid and model-predictive methods (Gallego–van Ryzin; Avram–Bertsimas–Ricard; Ciocan–Farias), claiming the first MCTS application to DRA problems motivated by real-world applications (pp. 1–3, 14).
writing: Main insights listed before each experiment block (pp. 7, 13); visual claims checked by regression tables (pp. 8–11); the fairness objection voiced in the authors' own words before it is tested (p. 12); §6.2 cites Table 7 for results in Table 6 (p. 13, my reading).
limits_future: MCTS hyperparameters interact and need tuning (pp. 3, 14); RHO needs the dynamics, though exactness mattered little here (p. 12); other DRA problems may differ (p. 12); no performance guarantees for either method. The edge is conjectured to track the action branching factor (p. 14).

method_links.note: Rival methods and two straw men dueled at matched budgets with significance tests, and the method with the information advantage handicapped to test fairness; no certificate of policy quality, and RHO's MIO solved to optimality only in most iterations.
The stochastic problem is replaced by a deterministic MIO approximation said not to be the original problem; the class is kept by smoothing, not by exact reformulation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: head-to-head study of rival paradigms at matched budgets with significance tests
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: MCTS against RHO with bracketing time budgets, straw-man baselines and regression p-values; S088 in this batch is a second case

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: handicap your own method to answer the information-advantage objection
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: RHO re-calibrated from 10, 100 or 1,000 sampled transitions instead of the true probabilities performs like exact RHO; absent from the 2014 version (S340)

transferable: When one method's run time cannot be capped, plot its time distribution and give the rival budgets that bracket it (60, 90, 120 s) (pp. 9, 11).
To test whether an information advantage drives the result, rerun your model-based method with parameters estimated from S sampled transitions (S = 10, 100, 1,000) (p. 12).
Fit additive-effects regressions of performance on method, instance size and their interactions, and report coefficients with p-values instead of reading box plots by eye (Tables 2–4, pp. 8–11).
coauthors: J. Daniel Griffith, Vishal Gupta, Mykel J. Kochenderfer, Velibor V. Mišić

quotes.text: One could argue that calibrating RHO using the true transition probabilities might unrealistically endow RHO with better performance
Initial evidence suggests this edge may be related more closely to action branching factor than the state space branching factor.
